summary: A person can make his animal's first baby holy as a different korban before it is born, so it does not become a bechor for the Kohen. If he says a male will be an olah and a female a shelamim, that is what they become.

chunks.en: How can a person plan ahead about a bechor?
chunks.st: How may one employ artifice to circumvent the obligation to give the firstborn to the priest and utilize the animal for a different offering that he is obligated to bring?

summary: If the animal gave birth to two males, one is an olah and the other is sold to someone who needs an olah. The same is true with two females and a shelamim. If it gave birth to an animal that is not clearly male or female, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it does not become holy.

chunks.st: and the second will be sold to those obligated to bring a burnt offering, who will sacrifice it as a burnt offering;

summary: If someone says the baby of his animal is an olah and the mother is a shelamim, both take hold. If he says the mother first, Rabbi Meir says the baby is just the baby of a shelamim, but Rabbi Yosei says it depends on what he meant from the start.

chunks.he: הָאוֹמֵר, וְלָדָהּ שֶׁל זוֹ עוֹלָה וְהִיא שְׁלָמִים,
chunks.en: If someone says, "The baby of this one is an olah, and it is a shelamim,"
chunks.st: One who says: The offspring of this non-sacred animal is a burnt offering and the animal itself is a peace offering,

chunks.en: his words stand.
chunks.st: his statement stands, i.e., is effective.

chunks.en: "It is a shelamim and its baby is an olah":
chunks.st: If he says: The animal itself is a peace offering and its offspring is a burnt offering,

chunks.en: it is the baby of a shelamim.
chunks.explain: Once the mother is a shelamim, so is her baby.
chunks.st: then since consecration of the mother preceded consecration of the offspring, it is the offspring of a peace offering, whose halakhic status is that of a peace offering;

chunks.en: These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: two names at once,

chunks.en: his words stand.

chunks.en: But if after he said, "This is a shelamim,"
chunks.st: And if it was only after he said: This animal is hereby a peace offering, that

chunks.en: he changed his mind and said, "Its baby is an olah,"
chunks.st: he reconsidered and said: Its offspring is a burnt offering,

chunks.en: it is the baby of a shelamim.
chunks.st: that offspring is a peace offering, as before he reconsidered, the offspring had already assumed the status of the offspring of a peace offering.

summary: If someone says an animal is the swap of an olah and the swap of a shelamim, Rabbi Meir says it is only the swap of the olah. Rabbi Yosei says that if he meant both from the start, both take hold.

summary: Saying "this is in place of that," "the swap of that," or "the exchange of that" makes a swap. Saying "this is redeemed onto that" is not a swap, but if the korban had a blemish, it is redeemed.
stIntro: This mishna discusses the language that serves to effect substitution.

chunks.en: "This is in place of that one,"
chunks.st: If one said: This non-sacred animal is hereby in place of that consecrated animal,

chunks.en: "the swap of that one,"
chunks.st: or if he said: It is the substitute of that consecrated animal,

chunks.en: "the exchange of that one" -
chunks.st: or if one said: It is the exchange for that consecrated animal,

chunks.en: this is a swap.
chunks.st: that non-sacred animal is a substitute.

chunks.en: "This one is redeemed onto that one" -
chunks.st: If he said: This consecrated animal is desacralized, with its sanctity transferred to that non-sacred animal,

chunks.en: this is not a swap.
chunks.st: that non-sacred animal is not a substitute.

chunks.en: And if the korban had a blemish,
chunks.st: And if the consecrated animal was blemished, and he said: This consecrated animal is desacralized, with its sanctity transferred to that non-sacred animal, the consecrated animal is desacralized

chunks.en: it goes out to be plain, and he must pay the difference in value.
chunks.explain: He pays if the holy animal was worth more.
chunks.st: and assumes non-sacred status, by Torah law. By rabbinic law, the owner is required to conduct an appraisal to ascertain the relative value of the two animals. If the consecrated animal was worth more than the non-sacred animal, he must pay the difference to the Temple treasury.
